themes.note: Isolation primitives first and platform programmes last: the order builds from the kernel mechanisms a container actually defends with to the incidents and governance that spend them.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/container-isolation-basics.md
steps.why: Namespaces and cgroups layered onto an ordinary process are the model every isolation decision in this Theme argues from.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/mount-namespace-basics.md
steps.why: The mount namespace holds the container's root filesystem, so it comes directly after the primitives that define what a container is.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/pid-namespace-basics.md
steps.why: PID namespaces explain why a container sees itself as process one and why host-side tools must name the namespace first.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/pid-one-signal-handling.md
steps.why: Signal handling only becomes a design problem once the PID namespace has made the container's first process special.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/network-namespace-basics.md
steps.why: The network namespace completes the isolation picture with interfaces, addresses, and sockets of the container's own.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/namespace-sharing-tradeoffs.md
steps.why: With all three namespaces understood, sharing any of them becomes an informed trade-off rather than a convenience.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/cgroup-resource-accounting.md
steps.why: Cgroups move from model to measurement: what the kernel charges the container for CPU, memory, and I/O.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/cpu-quotas-and-throttling.md
steps.why: CPU quota throttling is the first accounting figure operators actually feel, and it misreads without the accounting model before it.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/memory-limits-and-oom.md
steps.why: Memory limits fail differently from CPU quotas, and the OOM kill inside a cgroup is only legible with the accounting in hand.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/pids-controller-protection.md
steps.why: The PIDs controller bounds the one resource a fork storm spends, completing the cgroup controls before migrating them.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/cgroup-v2-migration.md
steps.why: Migrating hosts to cgroup v2 is safe only once the accounting, throttling, and controllers it reshuffles are understood.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/overlay-filesystem-copy-up.md
steps.why: Copy-up explains where container writes actually land, the filesystem fact every runtime tier below builds on.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/capabilities-least-privilege.md
steps.why: Dropping capabilities is the first concrete narrowing of what a container may ask its host's kernel to do.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/device-access-control.md
steps.why: Device rules govern the kernel interface underneath the capabilities, the second thing least privilege must bound.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/seccomp-profile-design.md
steps.why: Seccomp filters the syscall surface itself, the deepest of the three hardening mechanisms and last for that reason.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/readonly-root-filesystem.md
steps.why: A read-only root filesystem turns the copy-up and mount knowledge above into an enforced runtime policy.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/user-namespace-mapping.md
steps.why: UID mapping is the strongest answer to a container that needs root, and it presumes the capability and mount tiers before it.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/rootless-runtime-boundaries.md
steps.why: Rootless operation composes every namespace and capability lesson into a whole runtime, and its limits read only then.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/tenant-isolation-strategy.md
steps.why: Tiered isolation for multi-tenant platforms spends the whole primitive tier deciding what each tier of tenant may risk.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/runtime-hardening-baseline.md
steps.why: A baseline turns per-mechanism hardening into a versioned standard the exceptions below are measured against.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/privileged-container-exception.md
steps.why: Reviewing a privileged exception is the baseline applied to the one workload that refuses to meet it.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/runtime-exception-governance.md
steps.why: Governing exceptions across an organization replaces folklore with owners, expiry dates, and records.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/runtime-isolation-roadmap.md
steps.why: A multi-year roadmap prices the isolation tiers the platform will owe as its workloads and adversaries mature.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/container-escape-incident.md
steps.why: The escape response is the incident face of everything above: what was claimed, what held, and what to preserve.

steps.question: questions/advanced-containers/container-host-incident-readiness.md
steps.why: Readiness design closes the Theme by making escape response a rehearsed platform capability instead of improvisation.

themes.note: The reading spine walks the backend path first — stateless service, the API fork, the transaction sequence — before widening to the boundary questions and the portfolio tier that presupposes a running system.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/stateless-service-design.md
steps.why: The spine opens by naming what stays out of the request process, because every later pattern coordinates state that already left.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/synchronous-versus-asynchronous-api.md
steps.why: The synchronous-asynchronous fork is the first real design decision, and the queueing and outbox stages live on its asynchronous branch.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/rest-resource-semantics.md
steps.why: Resource-oriented endpoints settle the API surface before its failure modes arrive.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/authentication-authorization-boundary.md
steps.why: Separating authentication from authorization completes the surface and prevents the conflation the boundary questions would inherit.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/transaction-boundaries.md
steps.why: The transaction sequence starts here because the unit it defines is what retries and idempotency keys repeat.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/retry-backoff-and-jitter.md
steps.why: A retry is only affordable once the unit it repeats is short, which is exactly why boundaries come first.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/idempotency-keys.md
steps.why: Keys turn safe retries into a production contract for mutations, directly after the retry discipline they serve.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/transactional-outbox.md
steps.why: The outbox only makes sense once you have felt the dual-write it fixes, so it follows boundaries, retries, and keys.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/saga-compensation.md
steps.why: Compensation extends atomicity across services and presumes the outbox's guaranteed events as its transport.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/circuit-breaker-operations.md
steps.why: Operating the breaker after the retries it judges keeps the operator honest about what it masks.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/api-gateway-basics.md
steps.why: The gateway is the first boundary question, consuming the API surface settled at the start of the spine.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/api-versioning-policy.md
steps.why: Versioning and deprecation govern how the surface may change without breaking the contracts above.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/rate-limiting-policy.md
steps.why: Rate limiting protects the settled surface under load, a policy question once gateway and versioning exist.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/cursor-pagination.md
steps.why: Cursor pagination fixes the one read pattern offset paging quietly breaks at scale.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/multi-tenancy-isolation.md
steps.why: Tenant isolation widens the boundary questions from per-request correctness to per-customer state.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/background-job-contract.md
steps.why: The durable background job gives the asynchronous fork from step two its own operable contract.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/developer-portal-catalog-contract.md
steps.why: The catalog makes service boundaries discoverable, which only matters once those boundaries exist to publish.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/monolith-decomposition.md
steps.why: Decomposition opens the portfolio tier by re-cutting a running system along the seams the spine taught.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/platform-boundary-strategy.md
steps.why: Platform and product-service boundaries decide which side of each seam owns what, after decomposition shows what bad seams cost.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/cache-invalidation-strategy.md
steps.why: Invalidation for mutable data is the hardest boundary to hold and presumes the seam that owns the data.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/architecture-decision-portfolio.md
steps.why: A decision portfolio governs the record of choices the tiers above kept making implicitly.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/evolutionary-architecture-governance.md
steps.why: Evolutionary governance makes change itself a managed process rather than a series of surprises.

steps.question: questions/backend-architecture/resilience-investment-model.md
steps.why: Prioritizing resilience investments is last because it prices everything the Theme has built.

themes.note: Placement, TTL, and hit ratio come before invalidation and stampedes because every later mechanism tightens or backs up the contract a bound on wrongness sets.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-placement-layers.md
steps.why: Where the copy lives is the first of the three decisions every caching question ultimately reduces to.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-aside-basics.md
steps.why: Cache-aside is the pattern most services actually run, so it anchors the mechanics tier before any variation.

steps.question: questions/caching/read-through-cache-basics.md
steps.why: Read-through is the managed counterpoint, and the difference between them only teaches when placed side by side.

steps.question: questions/caching/ttl-selection-basics.md
steps.why: The TTL is the explicit contract for how wrong a value may be and for how long, set before keys or invalidation tighten it.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-hit-ratio-basics.md
steps.why: Reading a hit ratio honestly calibrates the mechanics before the policy questions arrive.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-key-design.md
steps.why: Keys carry the tenant and representation boundaries, so they precede invalidation — policy built on unsafe keys is wasted work.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-invalidation-policy.md
steps.why: Invalidation is the hard problem, and it needs safe keys and the TTL backstop already in place.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-eviction-policy.md
steps.why: Eviction governs what the cache keeps when memory runs out, the mechanical sibling of invalidation.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-stampede-control.md
steps.why: A stampede is what the invalidation and TTL model produces at expiry, so it follows them directly.

steps.question: questions/caching/negative-caching.md
steps.why: Caching failures and misses extends the same wrongness contract to values that are absent.

steps.question: questions/caching/redis-maxmemory-tuning.md
steps.why: Redis under memory pressure is where the operational tier starts, because eviction becomes an incident when maxmemory is wrong.

steps.question: questions/caching/redis-failover-operations.md
steps.why: Failover is the cache tier's outage rehearsal, and it presumes the tuning that shaped its steady state.

steps.question: questions/caching/memcached-slab-tuning.md
steps.why: Memcached's slab allocator is the counter-example that keeps Redis habits from hardening into folklore.

steps.question: questions/caching/multi-region-cache-coherence.md
steps.why: Multi-region coherence widens every earlier contract across distance and replication.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-capacity-cost-model.md
steps.why: The capacity and cost model prices the tier the coherence question just made global.

steps.question: questions/caching/cache-slo-degradation-policy.md
steps.why: SLOs that survive a degraded cache promise the degradation the tiers above rehearsed.

steps.question: questions/caching/shared-cache-platform-governance.md
steps.why: Governing a shared cache platform is the close, because a cache other teams depend on is a product.

themes.note: Definition and hypothesis before faults, faults before programmes: the order starts with what chaos engineering claims, ends with what it costs to run across many teams.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/define-chaos-engineering.md
steps.why: The definition, including why an experiment is not a test, anchors every experiment the Theme later runs.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/state-a-steady-state-hypothesis.md
steps.why: An experiment needs a falsifiable steady-state claim before it needs a fault or a tool.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/design-a-hypothesis-driven-experiment.md
steps.why: Designing the full experiment turns the hypothesis into a procedure with a written result.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/control-the-blast-radius.md
steps.why: Bounding the fault comes before injecting any, because every later fault assumes the bound holds.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/abort-a-running-experiment.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/inject-packet-loss-and-partitions.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/exhaust-cpu-and-memory.md
steps.why: Resource exhaustion moves the fault vocabulary from the network onto the host's own capacity.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/exhaust-disk-and-file-descriptors.md
steps.why: Disk and descriptor exhaustion complete the resource tier with slower and subtler saturation.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/run-pod-level-chaos-in-kubernetes.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/terminate-a-node-and-verify-recovery.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/simulate-a-zone-or-region-failure.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/choose-production-or-staging.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/run-data-layer-chaos-safely.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/facilitate-a-game-day.md

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/select-experiments-from-incident-history.md

steps.why: Cost justification prices the programme the practice has by now become.

steps.question: questions/chaos-engineering/run-a-chaos-engineering-programme.md
steps.why: Running the programme across many teams is the governance capstone the whole order built toward.
